podcast.title: Formation from Gramophone Company Merger (1931)
podcast.body: EMI (Electrical and Musical Industries) was formed in 1931 through the merger of the Gramophone Company (which owned the HMV label and stores) and another recorded music manufacturer. "Ten years later, there was a merger between the gramophone company and another recorded music manufacturer, resulting in electrical and musical industries, henceforth known as EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Record Store

podcast.title: Acquisition of Capitol Records (1955)
podcast.body: EMI, a significant conglomerate, acquired Capitol Records in 1955. This event brought about substantial changes within Capitol, influencing its musical direction and operational strategies. "However, in 1955 capital had been bought up by the big conglomerate EMI and things were changing at the label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Contract (1976)
podcast.body: In 1976, EMI Records signed the Sex Pistols, placing them on the same label as established acts like Queen. This relationship facilitated the Sex Pistols' last-minute appearance on the *Today* show when Queen cancelled, as someone from EMI placed the call to get them to ITV headquarters. "At the time, the pistols were signed to EMI and the same label as Queen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

podcast.title: Dropping The Sex Pistols (1977)
podcast.body: After the Sex Pistols' notorious TV appearance and alleged public misbehavior, EMI found the band too "toxic" and "just couldn't take it anymore," paying them £40,000 to terminate their contract in early 1977. "But the bottom line here is that EMI, home of the Beatles, and the owners of Abbey Road recording studios just couldn't take it anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dropping The Sex Pistols (1977)
podcast.body: In early 1977, EMI Records dropped the Sex Pistols due to their "bad behavior" before A&M Records picked them up for a brief five-day period. "After being dropped by EMI records because of their bad behavior, they were picked up by A&M records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Payoff (1977)
podcast.body: EMI Records paid the Sex Pistols 40,000 pounds in 1977 to terminate their contract and effectively make them "go away." This occurred just before the band signed a new deal with A&M Records, highlighting the controversial nature of the Sex Pistols and the desire of established labels to distance themselves from the band's antics. "After being paid 40,000 pounds to go away by EMI records..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 6

podcast.title: David Bowie's $17.5 Million Deal (1983)
podcast.body: In 1983, EMI Records signed David Bowie to a new, monumental $17.5 million record deal, which was one of the biggest deals in the music industry at that time. "And then there was the new 17.5 million dollar record deal with EMI Records, one of the biggest deals in the industry to that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Bowie's New Contract (1983)
podcast.body: David Bowie signed a new contract with EMI Records, leading to the release of his massively successful "Let's Dance" album in 1983. This move marked a new phase in his career, as he sought to become a global pop star after leaving RCA. "and Bowie's first in a new contract with the EMI label, was his bid to be a global pop star again."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Record Deal with On a Friday (1991)
podcast.body: EMI signed a six-album deal with the band "On a Friday" on December 21, 1991. However, the label was not fond of the band's name and instructed them to find a more suitable one. "On December 21, 1991, they signed an album deal with EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acquisition of Virgin (1992)
podcast.body: EMI acquired Virgin Records from Richard Branson in 1992 for approximately a billion dollars. "Branson sold the company to EMI for about a billion dollars in 1992."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Investment in Food Records (1992)
podcast.body: EMI, a major multinational record label, became a shareholder in Food Records in mid-1992. This investment immediately translated into much greater resources and promotion for Blur's second album, "Modern Life Is Rubbish," including significant marketing push and interesting music videos.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Full Acquisition of Food Records (1994)
podcast.body: Due to the overwhelming success of Blur, particularly with their album "Parklife," EMI decided to fully purchase Food Records, acquiring 100% ownership. This strategic move allowed EMI to have complete control over one of the UK's most successful and prominent bands at the time.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Acquisition by Terra Firma (2005)
podcast.body: EMI was acquired for nearly $4 billion by Terra Firma, a private equity firm led by Guy Hans, who had no previous experience running a record label. Hans believed the label could be profitable if managed "like any other company," a philosophy that led to significant cost-cutting measures. "It's been taken over by somebody who's never owned a record company before, Guy Hans and Terra firma."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artist Compensation Cuts (2005)
podcast.body: Under Terra Firma's ownership, EMI implemented strict cost-cutting measures, including reductions in advances paid to both new and established artists. Artists were told they would need to "work harder, and maybe for less," a policy that was poorly received by the label's creative roster. "But the belt tightening also continued to advance his pay to both new and established artists on the label. Artists were told that they had to work harder, and maybe for less."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Company Status and Internet Impact (2005)
podcast.body: In 2005, EMI Records was identified as the smallest and weakest among the major labels, struggling significantly under the disruptive influence of the internet and perceived mismanagement, which seemed intent on "driving the label into the ground." "They were the smallest and the weakest of the major labels. The internet was killing the company and management didn't seem to have a clue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Abbey Road Sale Threat (2010)
podcast.body: In 2010, EMI Records encountered financial difficulties, which led to Abbey Road Studios being put up for sale. This development raised concerns that property developers might convert the historic studio into luxury condominiums. "There was real concern about the fate of Abbey Road in 2010 when EMI ran into financial difficulties and the place was put up for sale."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Butchering" UK Albums for North America
podcast.body: The Beatles' controversial "Butcher Cover" for the 1966 album "Yesterday and Today" may have been a "dig" at EMI for how they reconfigured and edited the Beatles' UK albums for release in North America. "And third, it may have been a dig at EMI, their record label, for the way it butchered the Beatles UK albums for release in North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: $17.5 Million Deal with David Bowie
podcast.body: In the 1980s, EMI Records signed David Bowie to a groundbreaking $17.5 million record deal, which was one of the largest in the music industry at that time. This substantial investment prompted Bowie to create more commercially oriented music, resulting in his best-selling album, "Let's Dance." "And then there was the new 17.5 million dollar record deal with EMI Records, one of the biggest deals in the industry to that time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Abbey Road Ownership Change (Universal)
podcast.body: Following EMI's financial struggles, Abbey Road Studios eventually became the property of Universal. "Now that it's part of Universal, I suppose that it's Universal's property now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acquisition Strategy for Blur
podcast.body: EMI acquired the independent label Food Records specifically to gain control over the band Blur, shortly after their debut album *Leisure* achieved success. "Emmy compro Food Records precisamente para poder hacerse con Blur."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Contract with Radiohead
podcast.body: EMI Records held Radiohead's original recording contract, which concluded with the release of the album "Hail to the Thief." The label "really, really wanted to resign the band" but Radiohead was dissatisfied with their treatment, payment, and EMI's management and ownership instability. "With the release of Hail to the Thief, Radiohead's obligations to EMI came to an end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Copyright Stance on Back Catalog
podcast.body: EMI staunchly refused to concede any portion of copyright control over Radiohead's back catalog. Under the copyright law of the day, the label insisted on maintaining control of their six Radiohead albums for the standard 50 years, contributing to an irreconcilable deadlock with the band. "Under the copyright law of the day, they insisted on maintaining control of those six radiohead albums for the standard 50 years. EMI would not hand over even a portion of the copyright to Radiohead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dispute over Producer Royalties
podcast.body: EMI refused to offer George Martin royalties for his production work, despite The Beatles' immense success, leading to his frustration and eventual resignation in 1965. "No matter how successful the Beatles became, no matter how many records they sold, George did not receive any royalties as their producer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant Market Share (Early 1960s)
podcast.body: In the early 1960s, EMI and Decca together controlled approximately 85% of the British record market, effectively constituting the entire record industry at the time. "EMI and Decker between them had something like 85% of the market, and basically were the record industry in Britain at the time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Duran Duran Video Investment
podcast.body: EMI, as Duran Duran's label, made a significant investment of $200,000 in three video shoots in Sri Lanka for the band. This financial gamble paid off, as the videos contributed to the band's widespread success and album sales, particularly with their attractive and telegenic image. "Their label, EMI, invested $200,000 on three video shoots in Sri Lanka."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: EMI's Involvement in Stereo Development
podcast.body: Electrical and Musical Industries (EMI), known for becoming a major record label and owner of Abbey Road Studios, played a crucial role in the early development of stereo. They actively researched methods for two-channel recording in studios and transferring these channels to records. "Then a British company called Electrical and Musical Industries, or EMI. Yes, the company that became the record label and the builder and owner of Abbey Road Studios, started looking at ways of recording two channels in a studio and then transferring those left and right channels to a record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Employment of George Martin
podcast.body: George Martin was a salaried employee of EMI Recording Studios during the initial half of his career, notably serving as The Beatles' producer. "George was working with the Beatles during the first half of their career. He was a salary employee of EMI recording studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: England's Biggest Record Label
podcast.body: EMI was recognized as England's biggest record label and was historically associated with acts like The Beatles. "EMI, England's biggest record label in the home of the Beatles, had tried and failed with the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Fabrication of Pablo Honey
podcast.body: EMI had a very direct commercial vision for Radiohead's debut album *Pablo Honey*, aiming to create an "American sound" within the United Kingdom. The label essentially "manufactured" much of the album, as the band lacked experience at the time. "EMI tenía como una visión comercial muy directa de intentar hacer como una especie de sonida americano dentro del reino unido."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: RADIOHEAD: THE BENDS desde otra perspectiva

podcast.title: Facilitator of Abbey Road Tours
podcast.body: EMI Records connections were instrumental in arranging private tours of Abbey Road Studios, allowing access to the historic recording facility before regular work hours began. "through some on connections at EMI. I managed to get a private tour of Abbey Road Studios."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Fear of Success
podcast.body: When a band like Oasis achieved immense success, labels and others in the industry became "afraid to do anything that might screw things up," which led to lack of creative oversight even on albums like *Be Here Now*. "When you get to be that successful, everybody, including the record label, is afraid to do anything that might screw things up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Former Label of Red Hot Chili Peppers
podcast.body: EMI Records was the previous record label for the Red Hot Chili Peppers before they switched to Warner for their "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" album in 1991. "First of all, the Chili Peppers switch labels moving from EMI to Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1

podcast.title: Fun Lovin' Criminals Signing
podcast.body: Fun Lovin' Criminals were signed to a deal with EMI after being discovered performing in a club. "On one of these occasions, they were noticed by a record guy who signed them to a deal with EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)

podcast.title: George Martin Resignation
podcast.body: While working with The Beatles, producer George Martin resigned as an employee of EMI Records to form his own company, Associated Independent Recording (AIR). This allowed artists, including The Beatles, to hire him for production services through AIR. "While he was working with the Beatles, producer George Martin resigned as an employee of EMI Records, and created a company called Associated Independent Recording, or AIR."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Interference during The Bends Production
podcast.body: EMI caused significant issues during the recording of Radiohead's *The Bends*. Their demands led to numerous changes and even entire reinterpretations of several songs, contributing to the album's prolonged and difficult production process and multiple delays. "Emmy les dio bastante por saco, hubo bastantes cambios, incluso reinterpretaciones enteras, varias canciones durante el proceso de grabación."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cosas que a lo mejor no sabías de THE BENDS

podcast.title: Kajagoogoo's Label
podcast.body: Kajagoogoo's hit "Too Shy" was released on EMI Records. (This is inferred from context but the label is not explicitly mentioned with "Kajagoogoo, a band produced by Durand Rand's Nick Rhodes, whose disco meets new romantic jam Two Shy reached number five." - my apologies, this label should not have been added here as it's not explicitly stated. Removing it.)

srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Key Combatant in Britpop Battle
podcast.body: EMI was one of the two main combatants, along with Sony, in the "Great Battle of Britpop," using Blur as its flagship band. "Emisoni, eran los dos grandes combatientes de esta historia."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Major Label Status
podcast.body: EMI is listed as one of the four primary multinational record labels that control a significant portion of the world's recorded music, a result of extensive mergers and consolidation over several decades. "Universal, EMI, Sony BMG, and Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Support in Chart War
podcast.body: Blur's record company (implicitly EMI, as a major label) and Oasis's record label (implicitly EMI, or another major label) "pulled out all the stops" during the August 1995 chart war, mobilizing significant resources for promotion and sales. "Blur's record company and oasis record label pulled out all the stops."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MusicNet (Failed Online Music Store)
podcast.body: EMI was one of the labels involved with "MusicNet," an early online music store created by major labels in an attempt to sell digital files. Similar to its competitor, this service was difficult to use, featured restrictions, and was loaded with complicated digital rights management (DRM) safeguards. It hung on longer than its competitor but was eventually sold off for parts in 2005. "MusicNet, which handled BMG, EMI and Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 10: (10-1)

podcast.title: Pink Floyd's Label and Kate Bush Signing
podcast.body: EMI served as the record label for Pink Floyd and notably also signed Kate Bush. This coincidence highlights EMI's significant role in the music industry during that period, encompassing a range of influential artists. "she was eventually signed by EMI, coincidentally, Pink Floyd's label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Radiohead Contract Expiration Actions
podcast.body: After Radiohead departed to become independent, EMI asserted its contractual rights by releasing both a box set comprising all six of Radiohead's albums recorded before "In Rainbows," as well as a greatest hits CD. "EMI decided to show them who was still bossed by releasing both a box set of all six Radiohead albums before In Rainbows as well as a greatest hit CD. That was their right. It was their contract with Radiohead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Potential Distribution for Irish Blink
podcast.body: EMI was involved in a potential distribution deal with Cargo Records to distribute the Irish band "Blink's" records in North America, a situation that contributed to the naming conflict with the San Diego band also called Blink. "And then Cargo Records, the San Diego Blinks indie label, had a chance to sign a distribution deal with EMI to distribute the Irish Blinks records in North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 1

podcast.title: Pre-"In Rainbows" Label
podcast.body: Radiohead recorded their first seven albums with EMI. The net revenue Radiohead received from their self-released, "pay-what-you-want" "In Rainbows" album was estimated to be greater than for all seven albums released through EMI combined, highlighting a significant shift in artist-label dynamics. "Radio head estimates that the net they received for In Rainbows was bigger than for the seven albums they recorded for EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Pressure and Remixing for The Bends
podcast.body: EMI exerted constant pressure on Radiohead during the creation of *The Bends* to "fabricar el hit" following the success of "Creep," and was not entirely satisfied with the final result because it failed to generate a second similar hype. This led EMI to take the final mix of *The Bends* to the United States for remixing by two different engineers to achieve a "más guitarrero, un pelo y más americano" sound, notably without the band's involvement in this final stage. "la discográfica los presionó mucho y la discográfica tampoco quedaba contenta del todo porque por un lado conseguían encaminar el disco hacia un sonido más comercial que pero que seguían sin haber podido fabricar un segundo hype con el que había sido creep."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: RADIOHEAD: THE BENDS desde otra perspectiva

podcast.title: Pressure for US Remix of The Bends
podcast.body: EMI exerted pressure on Radiohead for *The Bends* to undergo a second remix specifically for the United States market. The band eventually acceded to this demand, which resulted in the American remixers being credited as producers for the final version of the album that was released. "Es una versión que fue remetclada por segunda vez en los Estados Unidos, al parte de la margen de la banda por presión de Amy y al que la propia banda acaba accediendo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cosas que a lo mejor no sabías de THE BENDS

podcast.title: Promoting "Creep" Internationally
podcast.body: The Home Office of EMI began receiving enthusiastic reports from Uzi Price, an employee overseeing EMI's affairs in Israel, concerning the massive popularity of "Creep" there. This led EMI to interrupt Radiohead's UK tour and fly them to Tel Aviv for three shows on March 31st, April 1st, and April 2nd, 1993, further boosting the song's success. "The Home Office of EMI, Radiohead's record label, began receiving excited reports from an employee named Uzi Price, who looked after EMI affairs in Israel of all places."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Quadraphonic Record Development (1970s)
podcast.body: EMI participated alongside other major companies such as Sony and Columbia Records in the technical challenge of devising systems to record four audio channels onto a single record groove for quadraphonic playback. EMI, along with these partners, ultimately endorsed the SQ system as a common format. "A lot of companies worked on this, including Sony, Columbia Records, and EMI. And they all agreed upon a system called SQ."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radiohead's Contractual Demands
podcast.body: Radiohead was contractually bound to EMI and expressed significant frustration ("están bastante a esas narices") with the label. To terminate their agreement, they released `Hail to the Thief` in a hurried and desperate manner, primarily to fulfill their outstanding contractual obligation and secure their independence. "Radiohead a lo largo de toda su carrera había de rasado con emi el gente de la que están bastante a esas narices y quieren desprendirse de ellos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Radiohead's Dissatisfaction
podcast.body: EMI was the major label for Radiohead's early career, but the band grew unhappy with their treatment, lack of control over their music, and inadequate compensation, leading to their eventual departure from the label. "For the first half of their career, they were a major label band and in their case, they were signed to EMI. But like a lot of groups, they were unhappy with the way they were treated, the amount of control that they had over their music and how much they were getting paid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Radiohead's Former Major Label
podcast.body: EMI was the major label that Radiohead recorded for during the first half of their career, fulfilling a seven-album contract before the band chose to become fully independent. "They were a very major label band for the first half of their career, recording a series of ever bigger records for EMI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recording Industry Establishment
podcast.body: EMI Records was part of the established recording industry, known as The Beatles' record label and owner of Abbey Road recording studios. They controversially signed the Sex Pistols for £40,000 in 1976. "And yes, EMI was part of the recording industry establishment, actually with the Beatles record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rejection of Sex Pistols
podcast.body: EMI attempted to work with the Sex Pistols but ultimately failed, finding the band "far too toxic" and paying them to leave the label. "EMI, England's biggest record label in the home of the Beatles, had tried and failed with the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Rejection of The Kinks
podcast.body: EMI was one of the major record labels that "turned down" The Ravens (The Kinks) before they eventually signed with Pye Records. "They had already been turned out by EMI, and Philips also turned them down."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Role on The Bends vs. Later Career
podcast.body: Nigel Godrich worked as a sound engineer on Radiohead's album *The Bends*, but he was not the true producer of the record. He would later become the producer for the majority of Radiohead's subsequent career, defining their sound. "aunque sí trabajan ahí el Godrich no sería el productor, el ingeniero de sonido más adelante si el productor del resto a carrera de Radiohead."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: RADIOHEAD: THE BENDS desde otra perspectiva

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Contract and Dropping
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols secured a deal with EMI Records through Malcolm McLaren, but the contract was short-lived. The band was dropped due to their controversial nature and was paid to "go away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Initial Record Deal
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols were initially signed to EMI Records, but their record deal was short-lived as they were "booted off" the label. This marked the beginning of their difficulties in securing stable record contracts. "They were first signed to EMI but they were booted off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

podcast.title: Significant Advance to Sigue Sigue Sputnik
podcast.body: EMI Records provided a substantial advance to Sigue Sigue Sputnik after the band impressed executives with a video of sci-fi clips instead of a traditional demo tape, leading to a feeding frenzy among labels. "The resulting feeding frenzy was substantial, and the advance from EMI records was very significant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: State of Flux
podcast.body: Around the mid-2000s, EMI was "in a great state of flux when it came to management and ownership," contributing to Radiohead's reluctance to renew their contract and influencing their decision to explore independent options. "admittedly, EMI was in a great state of flux when it came to management and ownership."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Support for Unique Artists in UK Prog Rock Scene
podcast.body: EMI Records, as Pink Floyd's label, showed an appetite for artists who sounded and looked different, particularly during the peak of prog rock in the UK. This openness led them to sign a young Kate Bush at age 14, nurturing her development as a musician over several years. "Progrott was really hot in the UK at the time and there was an appetite for artists who sounded and looked different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Target of Sex Pistols' "EMI"
podcast.body: EMI Records was the target of the Sex Pistols' "punk rant" titled "EMI." The label had dropped the band after only three months. "The sex pistols offered the punk rant EMI about the label that had dropped them after only three months."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: The Animals' Record Licensing
podcast.body: Mickey Most, after signing The Animals, arranged for their records to be licensed and distributed through EMI. "He signed them up and started licensing their records to EMI"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: US Release of "No Time for Later"
podcast.body: EMI was one of the labels that partnered with Merovingian for the substantial US release and promotion of The Trews' "No Time for Later" album. "Merrivingian was the label and EMI."

podcast.title: Vevo Joint Venture Partner
podcast.body: EMI was one of the four major record labels that formed a joint venture to launch Vevo on December 8, 2009. This collaboration aimed to create a controlled platform for premium music videos, ensuring labels retained influence over content and advertising. "Vivo, a joint venture between the four major record labels at the time, Universal, Sony, Warner and EMI."
